# Results — Study 283 (Hurricane-Season) on daily ^GSPC + an insurer basket

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The Atlantic
hurricane-season window (Jun 1 – Nov 30) and the major-landfall table are
hardcoded in [`data.py`](../hurricane_season/data.py). ^GSPC daily price-only
returns are from the repo-level cache (`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`); the
equal-weight P&C-insurer basket (TRV, CB, ALL, PGR, AIG, HIG, CINF, WRB) is from
the study cache (`_cache/hurricane_insurers.parquet`, total-return / auto-adjusted).
Match the fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC (split-adjusted, price-only, daily) | 1992-01-02 – 2024-12-31 | 8,311 days | `cd4c20c68e5d` |
| Insurer basket (8 names, equal-weight, total-return) | 1992 – 2024 | 8,310 days | staged cache |
| Major-landfall table | 1992 – 2024 | 30 landfalls | hardcoded constant |

Of the 8,311 market days, **4,205 are in-season** (Jun 1 – Nov 30) and **4,106
off-season** — the season really is ~half the calendar, which is why "avoid the
season" is a market-timing rule, not a free hedge.

## Broad market (^GSPC): in-season vs off-season daily returns

| Arm | mean (bps/day) | annualised |
|---|--:|--:|
| In-season (Jun 1 – Nov 30) | **+3.609** | +9.09% |
| Off-season (Dec 1 – May 31) | **+4.082** | +10.29% |
| **Spread (in − off)** | **−0.473** | −1.20pp/yr |

- **Welch t = −0.188**, **HAC (Newey-West) t = −0.214**, block-permutation
  **p = 0.802**. The in-season drag is −0.47 bps/day — statistically
  indistinguishable from zero by any test. The honest HAC t (the bar for a REAL
  verdict) is nowhere near |t| ≥ 2.

## Insurer basket (equal-weight P&C proxy): in-season vs off-season

| Arm | mean (bps/day) | annualised |
|---|--:|--:|
| In-season | **+5.971** | +15.05% |
| Off-season | **+7.097** | +17.88% |
| **Spread (in − off)** | **−1.126** | −2.84pp/yr |

- **Welch t = −0.332**, **HAC t = −0.350**, permutation **p = 0.692**. The insurer
  basket shows a slightly larger in-season shortfall than the market, but it is
  still pure noise at this sample size — and the basket is **survivorship-biased**
  (current members projected backward), so even this is an upper bound. Note the
  basket is total-return while the market arm is price-only; the level gap between
  the two is mostly dividends, not signal.

## Event windows around major landfalls ([-5, +20] trading days, 1-day lag)

| metric | value |
|---|--:|
| n events | 30 |
| mean insurer cumulative abnormal return (CAR) | **+0.248%** |
| CAR t-stat | **+0.329** |

Abnormal return = insurer-basket return − contemporaneous ^GSPC return (beta fixed
at 1), with a one-trading-day execution lag so nothing is earned on the landfall
day itself. The mean CAR around a major landfall is a *positive* +0.25% with
t = +0.33 — if anything, mildly consistent with the "gaining from loss" / hard-market
literature (catastrophes raise forward insurer pricing), and in any case
indistinguishable from zero.

## Could you trade it? — 'sit out the season' vs buy-and-hold (^GSPC)

| | annualised |
|---|--:|
| Buy & hold | **+8.35%** |
| Strategy (long off-season, cash in-season), gross | **+4.37%** |
| Strategy, net of 1 bp/switch (2 switches/yr) | **+4.35%** |

The timing rule earns barely **half** of buy-and-hold because it forgoes the equity
risk premium for ~half the year. In-season days still average **+9.1%/yr** — you
would be sitting out a perfectly positive market to dodge a drag that does not exist.
Transaction costs are negligible here (only two switches a year), so the verdict is
about the missing premium, not frictions.

## The n problem

Daily equity volatility is ~1%/day. To detect a true in-season mean shift at
|t| = 2 over ~4,200 in-season days you would need a structural gap of roughly
`1% * 2 / sqrt(4200) ≈ 3 bps/day` (~7.7pp/yr) **per arm** vs the off-season — the
observed market gap is −0.47 bps/day, ~15× smaller. For the 30-event landfall study,
~1% daily vol over a 26-day window gives a per-event CAR noise of ~5%, so the +0.25%
mean CAR is deep inside the noise floor.

## Positive control (synthetic)

With a planted in-season drag of **−10 bps/day** on the synthetic tape, the engine
recovers it cleanly (HAC t = −3.96, permutation p = 0.000); the −5 bps plant gives
HAC t = −1.55 (borderline, as expected); the null plant (0 bps) gives HAC t = +0.85,
p = 0.43. The machinery finds a hurricane-season effect *when one exists* — the real
tape simply has nothing like it.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Market in−off spread −0.47 bps/day (HAC t = −0.21, perm
  p = 0.80); insurer spread −1.13 bps/day (HAC t = −0.35, perm p = 0.69); landfall
  event CAR +0.25% (t = +0.33). No arm clears |HAC t| ≥ 2; survivorship on the
  insurer basket only flatters the result. There is no real hurricane-season signal.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The only implementation is "sit out half the year,"
  which earns ~half of buy-and-hold by forgoing the equity premium. There is no
  vehicle and no edge — costs are negligible, the opportunity cost is everything.
- **Busted — a calendar coincidence, doubly confounded.** Any apparent in-season
  weakness coincides with (and is more parsimoniously explained by) the documented
  Sell-in-May/Halloween window, and the insurer sign is theoretically ambiguous
  because catastrophes raise forward insurer pricing ("gaining from loss").
